title: DfE Decoded #156: School Food Is Becoming a Leadership Issue
author: A Headteacher's Perspective
summary: Writing as a serving headteacher, the author reads the confirmed revision of the School Food Standards and argues that its real significance is not nutritional but governance related. The standards now cover the whole school day rather than lunch alone, taking in breakfast clubs, breaktime, tuck shops, vending and clubs, which means a head cannot hand the change to a catering provider and assume it is dealt with. The piece walks through the specific primary breakfast and lunch requirements, from cereal sugar caps and bread fibre thresholds to a weekly pulses rule and a ban on deep frying the final dish, and concludes that for some schools this is a redesign rather than a tweak. It then makes the case that compliance is not success, because a technically perfect menu that drives a fifteen percent fall in uptake is not an improvement, and that pupil voice, taste testing and gradual introduction of unfamiliar foods are the real implementation work. The most urgent section concerns children with SEND, sensory differences and restrictive eating, where removing familiar items risks a vulnerable child accessing no school meal at all. The governance turn arrives at the end: a named lead governor for school food from September 2027, published policies and menus, a national compliance framework and monitoring data that may reach Ofsted.
points: The scope shift is the pivot of the argument, since separate breakfast standards arrive alongside a statutory duty to offer free primary breakfast clubs under the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026.

The author reads the consultation response as evidence that consultation actually moved policy, citing the dropped fruit-only dessert day, the raised cereal sugar ceiling and the phasing of secondary changes to 2028.
SEND and ARFID are treated as the near-term risk rather than a 2027 problem, with individual medical needs taking precedence over menu conformity.
The new lead-governor requirement plus published policies and menus is read as moving school food out of the kitchen and into accountability.
The closing reframe replaces the compliance question with an experiential one about whether children eat well, have time to eat, and return to class settled.
quotes: And I don’t think headteachers can simply pass this on to the catering provider and assume it is sorted.
They cover food and drink provided across the school day — including breakfast, breaktime provision, tuck shops, vending, clubs and other school food outlets.
Because there is little point in producing a nutritionally perfect breakfast that ends up in the bin.

Schools, parents and caterers warned that removing familiar foods too quickly could lead to children choosing packed lunches, buying food elsewhere, skipping meals or simply leaving more food on their plates.
But we shouldn’t end up in a position where a vulnerable child goes hungry because the only food they reliably eat doesn’t fit neatly into the standard menu.
From September 2027, the government intends schools to have a lead governor for school food.
The government’s own equality assessment notes that 81% of FSM-eligible pupils have a school lunch compared with 55% of pupils who aren’t eligible.
Because if these reforms achieve that, they will have done something much more important than change what’s written on the school menu.
